title: Tilak Varma Finds a Different Kind of Fun in India's Hardest Batting Job
excerpt: The vice-captain still loves No. 3, but his two-gear middle-order role is producing fifties and unbeaten finishes ahead of a Hyderabad homecoming.
body:
• Tilak Varma says he is enjoying India's middle-order role at No. 5 or 6, even though No. 3 remains his favourite position.
  • Two years ago he scored back-to-back hundreds at No. 3 in South Africa after Suryakumar Yadav gave up the spot for him.
  • His current brief has two gears: rebuild and bat deep if early wickets fall, or attack from the first ball if the top three bat into the 15th over.
  • The vice-captain plays his first home international in Hyderabad on Friday, in the fourth T20I against West Indies.

Tilak Varma has made peace with the hardest job in India's T20 side. The left-hander who announced himself with back-to-back hundreds at No. 3 now bats at No. 5 or 6 — and says the role, for all its difficulty, has become a different kind of fun.

"I love batting at No. 3 — I have said that many times," Tilak said on the eve of the fourth T20I against West Indies in Hyderabad, in comments reported by ESPNcricinfo. "At No. 3, you have the chance to bat in the powerplay when only two fielders are outside the 30-yard circle. So you can go and swing freely."

Two roles in one

The middle-order brief he now works to is really two jobs. If India lose quick wickets, he takes his time and bats deep through the middle phase. If the top three — Sanju Samson, Abhishek Sharma and Ishan Kishan — bat into the 14th or 15th over, he has to score from the first ball he faces. "Whatever the team needs, I want to step into that role," he said. "I am the man who always wants that pressure."

The numbers suggest the adjustment is working. In his last eight innings he has scored two fifties and finished unbeaten six times — the profile of a finisher rather than an anchor. Former India wicketkeeper Dinesh Karthik, himself a converted finisher, noted on Cricbuzz that a batter in Tilak's position can feel "a FOMO kind of a situation" watching the top order pile up runs, and credited him for delivering match-winning cameos anyway.

"Since childhood, my coach has taught me that whatever the role, whatever situation you are in, if you win the game for the team, it's a different kind of fun."

— Tilak Varma

Learning the hard way

The series has also given him a public lesson. In the third T20I in Indore, Tilak was run out for 28 off 16 balls in a bizarre mix-up: both he and Axar Patel assumed a shot had reached the boundary and relaxed mid-pitch while the ball was still live. Sunil Gavaskar called it "school boy stuff" on air. Tilak addressed it directly this week, saying he will never stop running even if an umpire signals a boundary — the kind of small discipline the finisher's role, with its older ball, slower surfaces and yorker-heavy bowling, demands on every delivery.

A homecoming in Hyderabad

Friday's match carries a personal edge: it will be Tilak's first international in front of his home Hyderabad crowd since he cemented his place in the side and became vice-captain. "It is a really proud moment that I am leading the Indian side as vice-captain and playing in front of the Hyderabad crowd," he said. "It will be a really special moment for me."

What's next

India's top-order riches mean Tilak's place in the XI is secure but his batting position is not — and he appears to have stopped fighting that. For a team still calibrating its middle order, a vice-captain who can rebuild at a run a ball or finish at two runs a ball, and who publicly owns his mistakes, is close to the ideal No. 5.
